questions.question: What is sediment, and how is it transported?
questions.expected_answer: Sediment is the small pieces of broken rock, such as pebbles, sand, silt and clay, and broken shells, made by weathering. It is carried away by rivers and streams, by wind that piles sand into dunes, by waves along beaches, and by glaciers in very cold places. As it is carried, the pieces rub together and become smaller and rounder.

questions.question: Explain how sediment settles in layers, and which layer is the oldest.
questions.expected_answer: Sediment is deposited when the wind or water carrying it slows down, for example when a river flows into a lake or the sea. Heavy pieces settle first and fine pieces last. It settles in flat layers, one on top of another, over thousands and millions of years. In undisturbed layers, the bottom layer was laid down first, so it is the oldest.

questions.question: Describe how layers of sediment become solid sedimentary rock.
questions.expected_answer: As more layers pile up, their weight presses down on the layers below, squeezing the grains together and pushing out water; this is compaction. Water carrying dissolved minerals seeps through, and the minerals form a natural cement that glues the grains together; this is hardening, or cementation. Over millions of years, the sediment becomes solid sedimentary rock.
